subjects.title: CCAF 3 - Prompt Engineering
subjects.description: Domain 3 (20%) - system vs user prompts, XML tags, few-shot, prefill, chain-of-thought, structured output, and sampling parameters.

cards.question: A document-extraction pipeline must return records that always validate against a fixed schema. What is the most reliable approach?
cards.answer: Define a tool whose `input_schema` is the target schema and set `strict: true` (or use structured outputs). Strict mode limits sampling to schema-valid output, so `tool_use.input` always matches the schema. A plain instruction is something the model can drift from. Note: the exam guide pairs the schema tool with a forced `tool_choice`. That still works on models that support it, but Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Mythos 5.1 reject forced `tool_choice` with a 400, so `strict: true` is the portable guarantee.

choices.text: Define a tool with `strict: true` and the schema as its `input_schema`
Instruct in the system prompt to output only valid JSON, then parse it
Validate the parsed text and retry the request whenever validation fails
Ask for JSON inside a fenced code block and extract the fence contents

hints: "Always validate" means you want a contract, not an instruction.

cards.question: You have a 40-page contract and one question about it. How should the prompt be ordered?
cards.answer: Long-form data at the top, the query at the end. Anthropic's long-context tips report that a query at the end can improve quality by up to 30%; putting the question first and burying it under 40 pages does the opposite.

choices.text: Contract first, then the instructions and the question at the very end
Question first, then the contract, so the model knows what to look for
Contract split into chunks, with the question asked after each chunk
Contract in the system prompt, question in the user message instead

hints: For long-context prompts there is a documented ordering. Which end does the question go?

cards.question: A classifier sometimes gets a ticket it cannot categorize with confidence and picks a category anyway. What is the best prompt-side fix?
cards.answer: Give uncertainty a representable value. If the enum has no escape hatch, an unsure model is forced to guess. Adding `unclear` plus a rule for when to use it turns a silent wrong answer into a routable signal.

choices.text: Add an `unclear` value to the enum and state when to use it
Instruct the classifier never to guess when the ticket is ambiguous
Send tickets that look ambiguous to a second, stricter classification pass
Add more categories to the enum so every ticket has somewhere it fits

hints: If the enum has no escape hatch, an unsure model is forced to pick something.

cards.question: Which prompt would you expect to be most reliable for a nuanced tone requirement?
cards.answer: Tone is easier to show than to describe. Diverse examples in XML tags outperform paragraphs of adjectives, and they also teach the edge cases.

choices.text: Three or four diverse examples of the tone, including one borderline case
Three paragraphs describing the tone, its register, and what to avoid
A single carefully written example, repeated so the pattern is unmistakable
A detailed style guide that the model reads before drafting each reply

hints: Tone is one of those things that is easier to show than to describe.

cards.question: A support agent must both reply to the customer in natural language and record a structured ticket. What is the cleanest design?
cards.answer: Use the right channel for each: prose text block for the human-facing reply, and a `create_ticket` tool call for the structured record. Forcing the reply into a JSON string field makes both worse.

choices.text: Text block for the reply, plus a `create_ticket` tool call for the record
One JSON object holding both the reply text and all the ticket fields
Two separate API calls that share the same conversation history
A prose reply with the ticket fields appended as a markdown table

hints: Two different audiences, so two different channels.

cards.question: An extraction prompt keeps inventing values for fields that are missing from the source document. What fixes it?
cards.answer: State the missing-field policy explicitly and make `null` a legal value in the schema, plus require the model to quote its source. Without an allowed representation for 'absent', the model fills the gap plausibly.

choices.text: Allow `null` in the schema, require null for missing fields, and require source quotes
Instruct the model to be accurate and never invent a value it cannot find
Mark every field required, so a missing value fails validation instead of passing
Re-run each extraction twice and keep only the fields where both runs agree

hints: The model has no legal way to say "this field was not there".

cards.question: Which instruction actually improves a review's precision?
cards.answer: Explicit, checkable criteria improve precision; general instructions about confidence or conservatism do not. The correct option states a test the model can apply; the others describe a disposition.

choices.text: "Flag a comment only when its claim contradicts the code's behavior"
"Be conservative and only report findings you are highly confident about"
"Check that comments are accurate and report anything that looks outdated"
"Report only issues a senior engineer would consider worth their attention"

hints: One of these can be checked. Three describe an attitude.

cards.question: One review category produces mostly false alarms, and developers are now ignoring accurate findings too. What is the recommended interim move?
cards.answer: High false-positive categories undermine confidence in the accurate ones, so the named move is temporarily disabling the category to restore developer trust while improving its prompt. The other options keep the noise in front of the same audience.

choices.text: Disable that category for now, while its prompt is being improved
Lower that category's severity so its findings stop blocking the merge
Keep it enabled but label that category as noisier than the rest
Route that category's findings to a separate report only leads review

hints: The damage is to trust in everything else, so the noise has to leave the report.

cards.question: Extraction of a required field returns empty for documents that use narrative prose rather than tables. What fixes it?
cards.answer: Adding few-shot examples that show correct extraction from varied formats is the named remedy for empty or null extraction of required fields. A retry cannot help when the model does not recognize the pattern, and it will fail identically.

choices.text: Few-shot examples showing correct extraction from both prose and table documents
A schema description saying the value may appear in prose or a table
A retry pass that re-sends the document when the field comes back empty
A separate extraction tool per document structure, chosen by a routing step

hints: The model is not refusing. It does not recognize the shape.

cards.question: What makes a few-shot example teach judgement rather than pattern-matching?
cards.answer: 2-4 targeted examples for ambiguous scenarios that show the reasoning for why one action was chosen over plausible alternatives - that reasoning is what lets the model generalize to novel patterns instead of matching only the enumerated cases.

choices.text: Showing the reasoning for why the chosen action beat a plausible alternative
Covering every category the model will meet in real production data
Using the longest and most detailed cases available in the training set
Presenting the examples in the same order the model will see inputs

hints: The alternative you rejected is part of the lesson.

cards.question: Invoice extraction validates against the schema every time, yet finance keeps finding totals that do not match the line items. What is happening?
cards.answer: The guide states it directly: strict JSON schemas via tool use eliminate syntax errors but do not prevent semantic errors - line items that do not sum to the total, values in the wrong field. Semantic validation is yours to add.

choices.text: Strict schemas eliminate syntax errors but not semantic ones like values that fail to sum
The schema types are too loose, so numeric strings pass where numbers were intended
The model is truncating the line item array when the invoice runs past one page
Validation runs before enrichment, so the totals are checked against stale line items

hints: The JSON is perfect. The arithmetic is not.

cards.question: A contract may or may not state an end date, and the schema marks `end_date` as required. What happens and what fixes it?
cards.answer: When a schema does not permit absence, there is no valid output that means "not present", so the model emits something plausible and wrong - and the pipeline accepts it. Nullable/optional fields are the named fix; a prompt rule cannot override what the schema demands.

choices.text: The model fabricates a plausible date; make the field optional so null validates
The extraction fails validation; add a retry that re-reads the document more carefully
The model returns an empty string; add a prompt rule forbidding invented values
The model omits the field; make the schema reject objects with missing properties

hints: There is no valid way to say "not in the document". So it says something else.

cards.question: A classification enum keeps meeting categories nobody anticipated. What is the recommended schema pattern?
cards.answer: The named pattern for extensible categorization is `"other"` plus a detail string. It keeps the enum's benefits for known cases while capturing the specifics of the unknown one - null would discard the information entirely.

choices.text: An `"other"` value plus a detail string field for the specifics
A free-text category field, validated against a list after extraction completes
A periodic schema update adding each new category as it gets discovered
A nullable category field, so unanticipated cases come back as null

hints: Keep the enum, and give the leftovers somewhere to say what they were.

cards.question: An extraction must run `extract_metadata` before any enrichment tool. How do you guarantee the order?
cards.answer: Forced tool selection ensures a specific tool is called first, with the subsequent steps handled in follow-up turns. `"any"` guarantees a call but not which one, and ordering by prompt is a request rather than a guarantee. Note: on Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, forced `tool` and `"any"` return a 400; there you use `"auto"` plus a prompt that names the tool.

choices.text: Force that tool on the first turn with `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}`
Set `tool_choice: "any"` and list `extract_metadata` first among the available tools
State the required call order in the system prompt and in each tool description
Give each enrichment tool a prerequisite field that only metadata extraction can fill

hints: You need a specific tool, not just any tool.

cards.question: Extraction fails validation because the due date is not in the document at all. What should the pipeline do?
cards.answer: Retries are effective for format and structural errors and ineffective when the required information is simply absent from the source. Continuing to retry burns budget and risks a fabricated value that finally passes validation.

choices.text: Stop retrying and record the absence, since retries cannot supply missing information
Retry with the validation error appended, which is the standard recovery path
Retry against a more capable model, which may locate the value in the layout
Retry with the document chunked differently, in case the field was split apart

hints: No amount of asking again puts the date into the document.

cards.question: What must a validation-retry request include to guide self-correction?
cards.answer: The named skill is a follow-up request including the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation errors. The error is the part that makes it a correction rather than another attempt.

choices.text: The original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation errors
The document plus a stricter instruction to follow the schema exactly
The failed extraction and the schema, so the model compares them
The document and the two nearest few-shot examples from the prompt library

hints: A correction needs to know exactly what was wrong the first time.

cards.question: Which workload is inappropriate for the Message Batches API?
cards.answer: Batch fits non-blocking, latency-tolerant workloads. A pre-merge check blocks a developer, and the batch window can run to 24 hours with no latency SLA.

choices.text: A pre-merge check that must pass before the pull request merges
An overnight audit of the previous day's support conversations
A weekly report summarizing every incident from the past seven days
A nightly job generating test cases for files changed that day

hints: Three of these run while everyone is asleep.

cards.question: Your per-document design calls a lookup tool mid-extraction and feeds the result back. Can it run on the batch API?
cards.answer: The batch API does not support multi-turn tool calling within a single request: it cannot execute your tools mid-request and return the results. The design has to be restructured or stay synchronous. Note: current batch requests can declare tools, and server tools such as web search do run inside a batch request; what is missing is your own code running a tool mid-request.

choices.text: No - batch cannot run your lookup tool mid-request and return its result
Yes, provided each request declares its tools and stays within the token limit
Yes, but only if every tool call happens in the first assistant turn
No - batch supports tools but not the JSON schemas the lookup would need

hints: It is not about limits or schemas. The capability is absent.

cards.question: Generated code is reviewed in the same session that produced it, and subtle bugs survive. What is the fix?
cards.answer: A model retains reasoning context from generation, making it less likely to question its decisions. Independent review instances beat self-review instructions and extended thinking - the guide names both of those as insufficient.

choices.text: Review with a second independent instance that lacks the generator's reasoning context
Enable extended thinking on the review turn so the analysis goes deeper
Add a review instruction telling the model to assume its own code is wrong
Split the review into per-file passes within that same generating session

hints: Two options ask the same session to think harder about itself.

cards.question: A review spans thirty changed files and produces shallow, sometimes contradictory findings. How should it be structured?
cards.answer: Splitting large reviews into per-file local analysis plus separate cross-file integration passes avoids attention dilution and contradictory findings. A single pass over everything is the arrangement that caused the symptom.

choices.text: Per-file passes for local issues, plus a separate cross-file integration pass
One pass per severity level, each hunting a single class of issue
One pass over the full diff, using a larger context window
One pass per author, so each reviewer's conventions are applied consistently

hints: Local issues and cross-file issues are different searches.

cards.question: Your document_type enum lists invoice, receipt, purchase_order, and contract. Roughly 8% of incoming documents are none of these, and the model forces them into the closest match. Which schema design handles this best?
cards.answer: An `other` value paired with a detail string keeps the enum usable downstream while staying extensible for the cases nobody enumerated. Free text loses the constrained vocabulary consumers depend on. Adding every type observed so far is a chase that never ends. Routing unmatched documents to a human sends away work the schema could absorb.

choices.text: Add an "other" enum value paired with a detail string that captures the actual document type.
Add every additional document type observed so far as its own enum value.
Remove the enum and let the field accept any free-text document type the model chooses.
Keep the enum and route documents that do not match any value to a human before extraction.

hints: Keep the closed vocabulary and give the model a legal way to say "none of these".

cards.question: Findings are split into four categories. Three are accurate, but the performance category is wrong most of the time, and developers have started dismissing all four without reading them. You need to keep improving the performance prompt. What do you do meanwhile?
cards.answer: A high false-positive category undermines confidence in the accurate ones, so turning it off while you fix its prompt is what protects the trust the other three still have. Posting it with a note explaining it is unreliable leaves the noise in the feed. Requiring two approvals to dismiss adds process friction to a bad signal. Merging it into security contaminates a category that currently works.

choices.text: Disable the performance category temporarily so the accurate ones regain developer trust.
Keep posting all four categories and add a note explaining that performance findings are unreliable.
Keep posting all four and require two approvals before a performance finding can be dismissed.
Merge performance findings into the security category so they inherit its credibility.

hints: One noisy category is training developers to ignore the three good ones.
